# estimation.joint { #wdm.estimation.joint }

`estimation.joint`

Phase 2: joint estimation of physiological state and metabolic parameters.

The idea is standard and worth stating plainly: append the unknown parameters to
the state vector and filter the lot together. The augmented state

$$
z_k = \bigl(\underbrace{T, F, G_c, G_n, A}_{x_k},\;
\underbrace{\eta}_{\text{parameters}},\;
\underbrace{\omega}_{\text{waist}}\bigr)
\in \mathbb{R}^{16}
$$

evolves with the physiological state following the energy-balance dynamics and
the parameter block following a slow random walk. Each morning's weigh-in then
updates *both* -- where you are, and what kind of metabolism produced that
trajectory. Parameter uncertainty contracts as evidence accumulates, which is
exactly the desired behavior when early food logs are less reliable than later
ones. The last two entries calibrate the optional tape measure (offset and slope
of waist against fat mass); they are personal constants like the metabolic
parameters and are carried and relaxed the same way, but they never enter the
dynamics. They are added only when some episode has a waist reading: the
unscented transform's sigma-point spread depends on the state dimension, so two
idle entries would perturb every other estimate slightly for no information.

Two design choices deserve comment.

**Why a random walk on parameters that are supposedly constant.** Giving the
parameter block a small process noise is what keeps the filter from locking in
early. With zero process noise the parameter covariance shrinks monotonically
and the filter becomes deaf to later evidence -- including evidence that its
early estimate was wrong. The random walk is a modeling fiction that buys
robustness, and it is also not entirely a fiction: maintenance energy genuinely
does drift with season, activity, and age.

**Pooling across episodes by sequential Bayes.** Episodes share your metabolism
but not your state: you started each attempt at a different weight with a
different glycogen load. So between episodes the physiological block is reset
from that episode's first weigh-in, while the parameter posterior carries
forward as the next episode's prior. Because episodes may be years apart, the
carried-forward covariance is relaxed back toward the prior at a rate set by the
calendar gap -- what your metabolism was in 2023 is evidence about 2026, but
weaker evidence than last month's. Past episodes without a food log are not
filtered here at all: they identify the noise in phase 1 and nothing else, and
filtering them would let a misspecified "intake unknown, near maintenance"
assumption bend the parameters (see the comment in `fit_joint`).

### JointFit { #wdm.estimation.joint.JointFit }

```python
estimation.joint.JointFit(
    episodes,
    transform,
    eta_mean,
    eta_cov,
    params,
    summaries,
    total_loglik,
    noise,
    waist_transforms=None,
    waist_eta_mean=None,
    waist_eta_cov=None,
    n_waist=0,
)
```

Result of phase 2.

``eta_mean`` and ``eta_cov`` cover the nine metabolic parameters only; the
waist calibration block is kept apart in ``waist_*`` so that everything
downstream of the metabolic posterior is unaffected by it.

##### maintenance_interval_kcal { #wdm.estimation.joint.JointFit.maintenance_interval_kcal }

```python
estimation.joint.JointFit.maintenance_interval_kcal(
    weight_lb,
    *,
    q=0.9,
    n_samples=20000,
    seed=0,
)
```

Posterior median and central interval for maintenance energy, kcal/day.

Returns ``(low, median, high)``.

This, and not the individual coefficients, is the quantity your data
actually pins down. The intercept and the mass slope are strongly
negatively correlated -- over the narrow range of body mass in one
dataset, raising one and lowering the other leaves the fitted trajectory
almost unchanged -- so each has a wide marginal posterior while their
*combination* at any particular weight is well determined. Quoting either
coefficient alone would overstate the uncertainty; quoting them as
independent would understate it. Propagating the full covariance through
the combination is the only honest option, and it is why this method
samples rather than adding variances.

##### maintenance_kcal { #wdm.estimation.joint.JointFit.maintenance_kcal }

```python
estimation.joint.JointFit.maintenance_kcal(weight_lb)
```

Estimated non-adaptive maintenance energy at a given weight, kcal/day.

Excludes the thermic effect of food and adaptive thermogenesis, so it is
*not* the intake at which weight would hold steady. Use
`weight_stable_intake` for that.

##### waist_summaries { #wdm.estimation.joint.JointFit.waist_summaries }

```python
estimation.joint.JointFit.waist_summaries(n_samples=20000, seed=0)
```

Posterior of the waist offset (cm) and slope (cm per kg fat).

##### weight_stable_intake_kcal { #wdm.estimation.joint.JointFit.weight_stable_intake_kcal }

```python
estimation.joint.JointFit.weight_stable_intake_kcal(weight_lb, tef_fraction=0.1)
```

Intake at which weight would hold steady, kcal/day.

Solves ``I = c0 + c1*W + tef_fraction * I`` for ``I``, i.e. accounts for
the fact that eating more itself costs energy to process. Ignores any
adaptation currently in effect, which if you are mid-deficit will make
this an overestimate of what you can actually eat without regaining.

### ParameterSummary { #wdm.estimation.joint.ParameterSummary }

```python
estimation.joint.ParameterSummary(name, mean, median, q05, q95, prior_center)
```

Posterior summary of one parameter in natural units.

Quantiles come from transforming Monte Carlo draws of the unconstrained
posterior, not from a delta-method linearisation. The transforms are
strongly nonlinear -- exponential and logistic -- so the induced posteriors
are skewed, and a symmetric interval would misrepresent them.

#### Attributes

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| [shrinkage](#wdm.estimation.joint.ParameterSummary.shrinkage) | How far the posterior median moved from the prior, in relative terms. |

### fit_joint { #wdm.estimation.joint.fit_joint }

```python
estimation.joint.fit_joint(
    episodes,
    cfg,
    noise,
    *,
    prior_scale=1.0,
    param_drift=PARAM_DRIFT_PER_DAY,
    substeps=4,
    spec=None,
    n_samples=20000,
    seed=0,
    dof=None,
)
```

Run joint state-parameter estimation across all episodes, in date order.

#### Parameters {.doc-section .doc-section-parameters}

| Name        | Type          | Description                                                                                                                                                                              | Default               |
|-------------|---------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------|
| noise       | NoiseModel    | Process and observation noise. The observation standard deviation should come from `~wdm.estimation.noise_id.identify_noise` rather than the default, which is a population guess. | _required_            |
| prior_scale | float         | Multiplier on the prior parameter covariance. Above 1 to express less confidence in the literature priors.                                                                               | `1.0`                 |
| param_drift | float         | Per-day random-walk scale on the unconstrained parameters.                                                                                                                               | `PARAM_DRIFT_PER_DAY` |
| dof         | float \| None | Student-t degrees of freedom for the observation noise, or ``None`` for Gaussian with the gross-error gate. Use the same choice as phase 1.                                              | `None`                |

### initial_body_fat_fraction { #wdm.estimation.joint.initial_body_fat_fraction }

```python
estimation.joint.initial_body_fat_fraction(cfg, weight_kg)
```

Body-fat fraction to initialize the fat-mass state.

Uses the configured value when supplied. Otherwise falls back to the
Deurenberg equation, which predicts body-fat percentage from BMI, age, and
sex. Its standard error is around 4 percentage points -- poor for a single
person, which is precisely why the initial covariance on fat mass is set
wide and why fat mass is reported with an interval rather than a number.

### state_frame { #wdm.estimation.joint.state_frame }

```python
estimation.joint.state_frame(fit)
```

Smoothed state trajectory as plain arrays, keyed by state name.
